title: Assessing the Accuracy of COVID-19 Information Circulating in a Facebook Online Community
screen_reason: Quantitative content analysis of COVID-19 information circulating in a public Brazilian Facebook online health community. Each of 108 evaluation items derived from the group's posts and comments was compared against DynaMed Plus evidence-based clinical summaries and coded correct / partially correct / incorrect / no available evidence. This yields a share of items in a sample judged inaccurate against an external ground truth (guideline concordance stated as accurate/inaccurate) with an explicit denominator, i.e. a CONTENT prevalence estimate.

estimates.country: Brazil (public Facebook group 'Eu ja tive COVID-19' / 'I've Had COVID-19'; Portuguese-language Brazilian community, Fiocruz authors)
estimates.platform: Facebook (public online health community group, >16,000 members)
estimates.measure_type: % of evaluated COVID-19 information items from a Facebook online health community classified as incorrect (contradicting the best available scientific evidence)
estimates.denominator: 108 assessment items and sub-items derived from the 136 posts and 2,156 comments published in the Facebook group between November 2021 and January 2022 (non-COVID messages excluded; 119 affirmative sentences merged to 61, expanded into 108 items)
estimates.definition: The item contradicted the recommendations of DynaMed Plus and was therefore coded 'incorrect'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "they propose redefining accuracy as the degree to which information aligns with the best available scientific evidence" (the paper's operative accuracy criterion; it also cites Allcott and Gentzkow's 'intentionally false and verifiable content designed to mislead a large audience' for 'fake news')

estimates.page_loc: Table 2, p. 7 (Analysis and Discussion of Results)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors converted posts and comments into affirmative sentences, then into a 108-item online assessment tool, and compared each item against DynaMed Plus (EBSCO) COVID-19 evidence summaries; four response options (correct / partially correct / incorrect / no available evidence), 'incorrect' = contradicts the platform's recommendations. Number of raters and any inter-rater reliability statistic are NOT reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The first phase of the study involved collecting posts and their corresponding comments published in the OC between November 2021 and January 2022. A total of 136 posts and 2,156 comments were gathered and systematically organized in a spreadsheet. After structuring the dataset, messages unrelated to COVID-19 were excluded from the analysis.
estimates.notes: denom_scope=topical + denom_selection=single_source because the corpus is the entire COVID-19 content of ONE Facebook group (one 'outlet') over a fixed window; sampling_frame=full_census because all posts and comments in the window were collected (the group itself was purposively selected for size, activity and open access). Country is not stated in a sentence but is unambiguous from the Portuguese-language group name, Brazilian authors/affiliations and the Brazilian pandemic context. year=2021 is the start of the Nov 2021-Jan 2022 window (midpoint December 2021).

estimates.country: Brazil (public Facebook group 'Eu ja tive COVID-19' / 'I've Had COVID-19')
estimates.measure_type: % of evaluated COVID-19 information items that deviated from scientific consensus (incorrect OR only partially correct) - broader definition of the same corpus
estimates.value_raw: 29.6% of the OHC's content (11.1% incorrect + 18.5% partially correct); 32/108
estimates.denominator: 108 assessment items and sub-items derived from the 136 posts and 2,156 comments published in the Facebook group between November 2021 and January 2022
estimates.definition: The item either contradicted DynaMed Plus ('incorrect') or aligned only partially with it ('partially correct'); the authors describe the union of the two as content that 'deviated from scientific consensus'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "they propose redefining accuracy as the degree to which information aligns with the best available scientific evidence"
estimates.source_quote: In our study, 29.6% of the OHC's content (11.1% incorrect + 18.5% partially correct) deviated from scientific consensus, exposing participants to health risks.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same procedure as the strict row: items compared against DynaMed Plus; 'partially correct' = 'Items aligning partially with DynaMed's data'. No reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Each tool item included four response options: correct, partially correct, incorrect, and no available evidence. We compared the content of each item to DynaMed Plus guidelines. We classified items as correct only if they fully matched the platform’s evidence. Items aligning partially with DynaMed’s data received the partially correct label, while those contradicting the platform’s recommendations were marked incorrect.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL. This is the broad-definition variant of the row above (same denominator). The 29.6% is stated VERBATIM by the authors (R8-compliant: it is the paper's own sum, not one I computed), but its numerator includes 'partially correct' items, which can in principle contain statements that are true yet only partially aligned with the evidence summary. Under the QUALITY-vs-CONTENT tie-break rule an adjudicator could reclassify this row as QUALITY; I kept CONTENT because the coding scheme is explicitly truth-oriented (correct / partially correct / incorrect) against an external evidence base and the authors themselves call the 29.6% content that 'deviated from scientific consensus'. borderline=true accordingly. Use ONE of the two CONTENT rows for pooling, not both.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) THEME-LEVEL SHARES NOT EXTRACTED. Table 3 reports accuracy by theme with separate denominators: post-COVID (39 items) 30.8% correct / 10.3% partially correct / 0% incorrect / 58.9% no available evidence; vaccination (31 items) 38.7% / 29.0% / 12.9% / 19.4%; infection (17 items) 47.1% / 5.9% / 23.5% / 23.5%. The abstract headlines three of these ('12.9% of vaccination-related content was inaccurate'), so an adjudicator may wish to add topic sub-rows (e.g. vaccination 12.9% = 4/31, topic=vaccines; infection 23.5% = 4/17, topic=covid19). I did not create them because they are nested inside the same 108-item denominator as the main row and would double-count in any pool; they are topic subdivisions, not separate countries/platforms/measures. All theme percentages check out exactly against the item counts. (2) NOT EXTRACTED, not misinformation: 34.3% (37/108) of items had 'no available evidence' in DynaMed - absence of evidence, not falsity. (3) NOT EXTRACTED: 'Across all themes, 63.7% of the analyzed information was either incorrect or lacked a scientific evidence base' - arithmetically inconsistent (11.1+34.3 = 45.4; 11.1+18.5+34.3 = 63.9), so I could not tie it to a defensible numerator. (4) NOT EXTRACTED: "The theme 'diagnosis' had the highest percentage of incorrect information (33%)" - denominator is 3 items, no table entry. (5) ABSTRACT/BODY CONFLICT: the abstract says 'only 47% of infection-related posts aligned fully with evidence-based guidelines' while the body says '47% of posts were either inaccurate (23.5%) or unsupported by evidence (23.5%)'; Table 3 shows 47.1% CORRECT, so the two 47% figures refer to opposite things (coincidentally equal). (6) The body twice mislabels tables ('As Table 1 illustrates, 34.3%...' is Table 2; 'Table 2 presents' is Table 3).

rob.design: Single purposively selected public Facebook COVID-19 online health community (>16,000 members), chosen on size, activity level and open access; census of all posts and comments published Nov 2021-Jan 2022 (136 posts, 2,156 comments); non-COVID messages excluded; content converted to 119 affirmative sentences, merged to 61, expanded into a 108-item/sub-item assessment tool; accuracy judged against DynaMed Plus evidence summaries on a 4-point scheme. No number of coders, no inter-rater reliability, no response/coverage rate, no sampling of other groups or periods; authors themselves note the single-group, single-period limitation.
